newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Burma, Cambodia, Laos to join ASEAN in July.
newsitem.headline: Burma, Cambodia, Laos to join ASEAN in July.

text.p: The Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN), shrugging off international pressure, decided on Saturday to admit its last three members -- Burma, Cambodia and Laos -- in July.
"It was unanimous. There were no reservations on the part of any ASEAN member," this year's ASEAN chairman, Malaysian Foreign Minister Abdullah Badawi, told reporters.

ASEAN -- grouping Brunei, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand and Vietnam -- decided last year to admit its last three members at some point this year. The group, founded 30 years ago as an anti-Communist bulwark at the height of the Vietnam War, had been under considerable international pressure to defer Burma's admission because of Rangoon poor human rights record.

Washington earlier this month imposed economic sanctions on Rangoon. Asked if Saturday's decision was a signal to the West that ASEAN would not tolerate pressure over the membership issue, Badawi said: "It was not a signal. We signal to nobody. We just made a decision on what is best for ASEAN and the region."
The group insists its policy of "constructive engagement" with Burma's generals would keep that country on the path toward democratic and free-market reforms.
In Rangoon, Burma's leaders hailed the ASEAN decision to admit it to the regional grouping in July along with Cambodia and Laos.

"Myanmar (Burma) has always placed confidence in the wisdom of the leaders of ASEAN member nations for the acceptance of Myanmar (Burma), Cambodia and Laos into the prestigious association of the region," a government spokesman told Reuters.

Burma's authorities planned to block entry to democracy leader Aung San Suu Kyi's home and blockade her party's headquarters until after the ASEAN meeting to avoid clashes, an official source said in Rangoon on Friday.

Suu Kyi, in a taped interview that was smuggled out of the country and released on Thursday, said Burma's military rulers could become "even more obdurate and oppressive" if the country were admitted to ASEAN.
She said Burma under the military regime would be no credit to ASEAN, and urged constructive engagement with her party.

Asked if ASEAN decided to admit Burma now before the human rights situation there worsens, Badawi said: "Anything can happen. But we think we can deal more effectively when Myanmar (Burma) is a member of ASEAN."
ASEAN officials have also privately expressed concern over the strategic need to pull Burma out of China's orbit.

That was underlined on Friday when the official media in Rangoon reported that Burma has signed a broad economic and trade cooperation agreement with China, a move coming soon after the U.S. sanctions.

The reports said China's visiting vice minister for foreign trade and economic cooperation, Li Guo Hua, and Burma's national planning minister, David Abel, also agreed on Thursday to form a joint works committee for cooperation.

China is one of Burma's closest allies and is said to be its biggest supplier of weapons. Indonesian Foreign Minister Ali Alatas referred to the strategic importance of the new members on Saturday. "I think we are also taking into account the overall and long-term consideration of peace and security and tranquility in our part of the world," Alatas told reporters. "So by having all three enter...we are complete now. And we are in a better position in ASEAN to contribute to peace and stability in our own region as well as in the larger region of East Asia."

The induction of the three new members will take place at ASEAN's annual ministerial meeting in Kuala Lumpur on July 24-25. A new logo, featuring 10 rice stalks representing all 10 of Southeast Asian nations would be unveiled then.
